interactionPlan.concept: The physical geometry of an occluder determines the conditioning and noise-sensitivity of the light transport matrix used to reconstruct a scene.
learningObjectives: Understand how different physical occluders (knife-edges vs. pinholes) map scene elements to camera sensor pixels using a light transport matrix A
Explain why a knife-edge occluder leads to a triangular transport matrix that acts as an integrator
Identify how the mathematical inversion of an integrating transport matrix amplifies high-frequency noise
Articulate the fundamental computational imaging trade-off between light throughput and reconstruction stability
interactionPlan.keyInsight: An edge occluder lets in far more light than a tiny pinhole, but reconstructing the scene requires differentiating the sensor signal, which dramatically amplifies noise due to an ill-conditioned inverse matrix.

interactions.label: Occluder Geometry
interactions.effect: Toggles the physical scene layout and transport matrices between (a)/(b) the Edge Occluder (integrating wedge) and (c)/(d) the Pinhole/Slit.
interactions.teaches: How physical changes in aperture shape directly transform the light transport matrix A from triangular to diagonal.

interactions.label: Sensor Noise
interactions.effect: Adds random noise to the simulated camera sensor measurement, displaying the resulting reconstructed scene alongside the mathematical inversion.
interactions.teaches: Why the high-frequency checkerboard patterns in the inverse matrix A-1 lead to catastrophic noise amplification for the edge camera, but not for the pinhole.

demo_steps.title: Mapping Light with Matrices
demo_steps.narration: Look at the edge occluder setup on the left. The scene points at the top map to the sensor pixels at the bottom. Because the half-plane blocks only part of the light, each sensor pixel receives a wide 'wedge' of light (green and orange zones). This overlapping mapping is represented by the lower-triangular light transport matrix A, where each row represents a sensor pixel integrating light from a progressive range of scene elements.
demo_steps.focus: The triangular shape of matrix A and the overlapping light wedges reaching the sensor in diagram (a).

demo_steps.title: The Inversion Trap
demo_steps.narration: To recover the original scene, we must mathematically invert this integration using the inverse matrix A-1. Notice the checkerboard-like alternating black and white pattern in A-1. This pattern means the reconstruction algorithm must subtract adjacent sensor values to find the differences. If there is absolutely zero noise, this inversion works perfectly.
demo_steps.focus: The alternating high-frequency patterns of the inverse matrix A-1 in panel (b).

demo_steps.title: How Noise Destroys the Edge Camera
demo_steps.narration: Now, slowly increase the sensor noise slider. Notice how even a tiny amount of noise completely corrupts the reconstructed scene. Because matrix A-1 subtracts neighboring pixels, any random difference between them is amplified into wild, high-frequency noise spikes, rendering the edge camera highly unstable in real-world conditions.
demo_steps.focus: The rapid degradation of the reconstructed scene image as noise is introduced, driven by the ill-conditioned A-1 matrix.

demo_steps.title: The Stable Pinhole Alternative
demo_steps.narration: Switch the occluder geometry to the Pinhole. Notice that matrix A is now a clean diagonal line because each sensor pixel maps to exactly one narrow ray from the scene. Because there is no overlap, the inverse matrix A-1 is also diagonal. Try raising the noise slider here: the noise in the reconstructed scene increases only linearly, without any catastrophic amplification.
demo_steps.focus: The diagonal structure of matrices A and A-1 in panel (d) and the relative stability of the reconstruction under noise.

demo_steps.title: The Fundamental Imaging Tradeoff
demo_steps.narration: Compare the two designs: the edge occluder lets in massive amounts of light (high SNR before reconstruction) but is mathematically unstable to invert. The pinhole camera is mathematically robust and simple to invert, but discards over 99% of the available light. Modern computational imaging design is a constant search for the sweet spot between these two extremes.
demo_steps.focus: The overall visual contrast between the broad light wedges of the edge camera and the narrow, light-starved rays of the pinhole.

interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: The visualization should be split into two main view modes toggled by 'occluderType'. The left panel shows the 2D ray geometry: a top scene bar with small square elements, a bottom sensor bar with square elements, an occluder in the middle, and colored light cones (green for general field of view, orange highlighting a specific pixel's field of view). The right panel shows three grayscale matrix grids stacked vertically: the forward transport matrix A, the analytical inverse A-1, and a regularized/conditioned version B. The 'edge' mode displays a lower-triangular matrix for A, a stark checkerboard-diagonal pattern for A-1, and a smoothed band for B. The 'pinhole' mode displays a tight diagonal band for A, a slightly wider diagonal with minimal checkerboarding for A-1, and a clean diagonal for B. An interactive live graph plotting 'Original Scene' vs 'Reconstructed Scene' should react to the 'noiseLevel' slider to dramatically demonstrate the difference in noise amplification.
